articles.title: Everything Else Is Noise review – a musician attempts to raise her art above the cacophony of city noise
articles.description: A TV shoot is beset with barking dogs, power cuts and personal animosities in Nicolás Pereda’s docufiction exploring the fight for artistic space in a world of distractions This latest docufiction from Mexican-Canadian film-maker Nicolás Pereda finds rhythm amid chaos. The film opens with an amusing visual game of Tetris; at a busy intersection in Mexico City, the concept of designated lanes and traffic signals appears to be symbolic only. Here, driving is all about carving your own path, as crisscrossing cars squeeze their way past each other. Reminiscent of Jacques Tati’s ending to Playtime (1967), this entrancing dance of machines encapsulates Pereda’s central dilemma: the question of seizing one’s personal and artistic space amid a world of distractions. The cacophony of honks and revving engines is accompanied by an expressionistic cello piece, played by a composer called Teresa (played by Teresita Sánchez). To some of her neighbours, however, her music is no different from the traffic noise. On this particular day, Teresa has opened her home to fellow musician Rosa (Rosa Estela Juárez Vargas), who wants to use the space for her interview with a two-man television crew. From a nearby dog’s loud barking to intermittent power cuts, the shoot is beset with continual interruptions; but the film also foregrounds the subtle frictions that grow between the characters. Panning shots swing from the banal questions posed by the male interviewers to the women’s unimpressed faces. We can sense that this is not the first time they have been faced with mediocrity. articles.title: The Song of Stork and Dromedary by Anjet Daanje review – don’t miss this glorious epic inspired by Emily Brontë
articles.description: The afterlife of a Yorkshire village girl who becomes a gothic literary icon is explored across three centuries, in a thrilling paean to the power of books I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation. We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.” Continue reading...
